title: How do you handle request aggregation in an API Gateway when multiple services must be queried (parallel WebClient + `Mono.zip`)?
shortTitle: Handling request aggregation when multiple services must be queried
keyPoints: Request aggregation lets the gateway call several backend services and compose one response for the client.
Non-blocking WebClient returns a Mono without blocking the thread, enabling concurrent downstream calls.
Mono.zip combines multiple Monos and completes when all inputs complete, giving a tuple of results.
Total time is the slowest single call, not the sum of all calls, because they run in parallel.
Each downstream call needs its own timeout and fallback so one dead service does not blank the whole response.
For a variable number of calls, use Flux.flatMap with bounded concurrency instead of Mono.zip.
Keep aggregation simple and view-oriented at the gateway; heavy business aggregation belongs in a dedicated service.

s1_definition.oneliner: Fire the downstream calls in parallel with non-blocking WebClient, combine them with Mono.zip, and the client gets one aggregated response in the time of the slowest single call, not the sum.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Request aggregation** – the gateway responds to a single client call by querying several backend services and composing their responses into one payload.
- **WebClient** – the reactive, non-blocking HTTP client in Spring WebFlux that returns a `Mono` without tying up a thread.
- **Mono.zip** – a combinator that takes multiple Monos, subscribes to them concurrently, and emits a tuple when all complete.
- **Parallel execution** – because the Monos are independent, total time equals the slowest call, not the sum.
- **Per-call resilience** – each downstream call gets its own timeout and fallback so a failed service degrades gracefully rather than killing the aggregate.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh asks the National Bank of India help desk for a complete summary: his account balance, his card status, and his recent payments. A slow clerk would walk to the accounts room, come back, then walk to the cards room, come back, then walk to the payments room, taking three trips end to end. A smart clerk sends three runners at the same time, waits at the desk until all three return, and staples their papers into one summary sheet. The gateway doing Mono.zip over three parallel WebClient calls is that smart clerk.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Request aggregation is when the gateway responds to a single client call by querying several backend services and composing their answers into one payload. The whole point is to turn a chatty client, which would make many round trips, into one call, and to do the backend work in parallel. In a reactive Spring Cloud Gateway or WebFlux service, the tool for this is the non-blocking WebClient combined with Mono.zip.

The key is concurrency. The wrong way is to call each service sequentially and block between them, because then the total time is the sum of all latencies and you tie up a thread the whole time. The correct way starts all WebClient calls concurrently, each returning a Mono, and combines them with Mono.zip, which completes when all inputs complete. Because the calls overlap, the total time is the slowest single call, not the sum.

At National Bank of India, the mobile dashboard for Rajesh needs account, card, and payment data from three services. The gateway aggregates them in parallel, so the app makes one call and gets one response in about 120ms instead of 300ms. The part that makes it production-grade is per-call resilience: each downstream call has its own timeout and fallback, so when the card service was briefly down, the dashboard still showed account and payment data while the card section showed "unavailable."

Remember one sentence: use Mono.zip with per-call timeouts and fallbacks to aggregate parallel WebClient calls into one response, so the client gets one fast call instead of many slow ones.
